title: The Set Interface
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of the set interface and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.
Apply at least one of the lesson topics—unique elements—in a small, readable example.
Predict the example result and check it against the stated output or a boundary-case test.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study the set interface with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you select data structures according to ordering, uniqueness, lookup, and update needs. In this lesson, focus on unique elements and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Choose a collection by its contract: ordering, uniqueness, key lookup, insertion/removal cost, and iterator behavior. Do not assume every implementation preserves order or supports concurrent mutation. Apply that reasoning specifically to unique elements and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect unique elements with membership testing before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

items.title: Membership testing
items.text: A good test states the behavior it verifies and isolates the cause of a failure. Include boundary and error cases; coverage alone does not prove that assertions are meaningful.

items.title: Equality and uniqueness
items.text: Choose a collection by its contract: ordering, uniqueness, key lookup, insertion/removal cost, and iterator behavior. Do not assume every implementation preserves order or supports concurrent mutation. Apply that reasoning specifically to equality and uniqueness and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test.

items.title: Choosing appropriate set implementations
items.text: Choose a collection according to ordering, uniqueness, lookup, and update requirements. Review equals/hashCode contracts, iteration behavior, and concurrent-modification rules before selecting an implementation.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Choose a set when uniqueness is the important property; iteration order depends on the implementation. For ordinary Java SE examples, use JDK 25, save a complete class as Main.java, and run `javac Main.java` followed by `java Main`. CodeLeaf does not execute Java in the browser; use a local JDK for these examples. Preview-only and configuration-file examples have their own version or filename notes.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, remove any temporary output files it created, and rerun the baseline case. Do not leave credentials, generated private data, or large test files in the project directory.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.

content.task: Try it yourself: build the smallest program that demonstrates unique elements. Change one input, predict the result, and add one boundary or invalid case before considering the task complete.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates at least one listed topic from The Set Interface.
The learner states the expected result before running or inspecting the example.
At least one boundary, failure, compatibility, or maintainability consideration is documented where relevant.
hints: Start by identifying the contract or rule behind unique elements.
Reduce the example to the smallest input that makes the behavior visible.
Test one boundary or failure case and compare the result with the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Applying the rule from memory without checking its exact contract.
common_mistakes.why: Small differences in type, scope, API version, or input shape can change the result.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the relevant official API/language documentation and build a minimal reproducer.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only a single happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Boundary values and failures often reveal assumptions hidden by the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add an empty, boundary, or invalid case and state the expected behavior before running it.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify the actual cause of a different result.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one factor at a time and keep a short record of observed behavior.

summary: The Set Interface is best understood by connecting its contract to a small observable example.
Key syllabus points: Unique elements, Membership testing, Equality and uniqueness.
Use official versioned documentation and tests to confirm assumptions before relying on behavior in a larger application.
